issues.legal_issue: Fishing permits issued to settle traditional claims before completion of the protected-area notification process were not governed by the general power to regulate fishing within a protected area.
material_facts: The area had been declared for intended inclusion in a national park, but the final notification had not been issued.
Although no claims were lodged after the initial proclamation, the government later received claims that displaced tribal residents had traditionally fished for their livelihood.
The district collector reported that fishing was the principal livelihood of affected families and that they had not been systematically rehabilitated.
The State considered the traditional fishing rights unsettled and issued permits in their settlement before the final notification.
issues.conclusion: The permits were issued in settlement of traditional fishing rights before the final notification and therefore did not fall under the general fishing-control provision; they were not set aside on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 35(3) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the claims process in Sections 19 to 26 applies to a proposed national park, and Section 35(4) provides for the final notification after claims have been disposed of and rights have vested in the State. Section 33(e), as it stood before its deletion in 1991, empowered the Chief Wildlife Warden to regulate, control or prohibit fishing. The Court held that permits issued in settlement of traditional fishing rights before the final notification did not fall under Section 33. The petitioner relied on Sections 5 and 26(1)(j) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, but the Court’s decision rested on the unresolved traditional claims and the timing and purpose of the permits.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_fishing_per: An association brought a public-interest proceeding challenging permits authorizing fishing in a protected-area setting.
predicates.traditional_fishing_claims_unsettled: The government considered claims of traditional fishing rights unresolved after affected residents later asserted those claims.
predicates.permits_issued_before_final_protected_ar: The government issued fishing permits before completing the final notification process for the protected area.

issues.definition: When a public-interest challenge concerns fishing permits issued before final protected-area notification to address unresolved traditional fishing claims, the permits are not subject to the general park fishing-control provision.

issues.legal_issue: Fishing permits in a sensitive protected area may be maintained only with safeguards sufficient to limit ecological harm and control permit holders’ activities.
material_facts: The permits allowed a large number of fishers to enter a reservoir in the heart of a national park and tiger reserve.
The petitioner and a neighboring State identified risks to biodiversity, fish, reptiles, water birds and migratory birds, as well as risks of poaching, tree damage, fires and littering.
The Court accepted the concern that monitoring all permit holders and preventing harmful conduct would be difficult.
Existing permit conditions restricted the season, entry times, route and access to islands, but the Court considered additional directions necessary.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the permits subject to detailed controls, including personal non-transferable permits, restricted access and travel, demarcation of fishing areas, check posts, daily records, prohibitions on fires and littering, and adequate monitoring personnel, vehicles and boats.
issues.legal_principle: The Court balanced the need to protect the fragile ecology and wildlife of the protected area against the displaced residents’ need to earn a livelihood. It relied on the environmental duties reflected in Articles 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution and on the protective purpose of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. In Pradeep Krishen v. Union of India, AIR 1996 SC 2040, the Court had emphasized that India could not afford further shrinkage of its forest cover and that urgent steps were needed to prevent damage to protected areas.

predicates.fishing_permitted_in_ecologically_sensit: The government authorized fishing in an area containing protected wildlife and habitat.

issues.definition: When a public-interest challenge concerns fishing in an ecologically sensitive protected area and permit holders pose substantial risks that are difficult to monitor, the permits may be maintained only with strict ecological controls.

issues.legal_issue: The State must complete the final protected-area notification process expeditiously once claims concerning the area have been addressed.
material_facts: The State had published its intention to constitute the area as a national park and collectors had issued final orders after inviting claims.
The State had received and considered later claims of traditional fishing rights and had issued permits in their settlement.
The final notification specifying the national park area had still not been issued.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the State to issue the final notification expeditiously.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35(4) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 provides for the final notification after the claims process is completed and rights in the proposed area have vested in the State. The Court stressed the duties under Articles 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution to protect the environment, forests and wildlife. It also relied on Pradeep Krishen v. Union of India, AIR 1996 SC 2040, regarding the need to prevent further shrinkage of forest cover and to act urgently to protect forests and wildlife.

issues.definition: When a public-interest proceeding concerns a proposed protected area, its claims have been addressed and the final notification remains unissued, the government must expedite that notification.
